correctness.rationale: All definitions quantify over two agents, an integer T>=1 and every ordered pair of perfect matchings. At optimal T, exact coverage by utility-contributing disjoint pairs forces whole alternating-cycle assignments, and each removed item destroys exactly one of the evaluator’s opposite-color pairs. This proves the necessary/sufficient near-balanced subset condition for both EF1 and EFX. If absent, a maximum-length component L>=2 is split into L−1 disjoint recipient-valued pairs and two leftover goods, with pair-count difference at most one after greedy assignment of the other components. Giving the two leftovers to the lower-count recipient makes EFX follow from floor((bundle_size−1)/2) upper bounds. The resulting T−1 welfare matches the universal upper bound in that case; DP reconstructs either case. Separate exhaustive enumeration of 11,260 matching-pair instances with 2–8 goods checks construction and EFX inequalities. Finite checks are corroborative and do not replace the all-size proof.

value.rationale: Pairwise complements are a central example motivating the 2026 fair-allocation model. A finite four-item impossibility alone was previously known, but it left the efficiency behavior of two fully covering complement lists at arbitrary size unresolved in the inspected source. The cycle-decomposition theorem supplies a complete exact decision criterion for zero fairness cost versus the unavoidable single-unit loss, a witnessing efficient construction, an O(T²) algorithm and quantitative near-total welfare. This is a motivated structural classification of a natural class rather than an arbitrary fixed-size enumeration or cosmetic restatement of the known example.
